governanceNotes: D1 batch 51 (2026-09-24): deferred. Course and synonym-identity screens recorded 2026-09-24: the catalog identity is Laryngitis with the alias 'acute laryngitis', and acute laryngitis is a self-limited mucosal infection whose located literature reports symptom-level voice impairment (dysphonia, hoarseness, cough, dry throat) rather than a distinct downstream catalog diagnosis; the chronic form is a separately published identity whose own authored window runs chronic-laryngitis -> vocal-cord-nodules-polyps-cysts-paralysis, so an acute-to-chronic progression edge would restate the same disease process under two identity names and create a parallel pathway - the disposition pattern already applied to eczema, iritis, intervertebral-disc-syndrome, and other synonym and parallel-pathway pairs in this program.

Evidence-ground screens recorded 2026-09-24: the located candidate propositions were reviewed and rejected rather than authored. Aphonia: the retrieved aphonia evidence concerns unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis (with flaccid vocal fold and paralytic aphonia) and functional laryngeal disorders such as paradoxic vocal fold motion rather than laryngitis. Laryngospasm: the located prevalence cohort is amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis-specific, where laryngospasm was reported in 4% of 571 patients with excessive saliva irritating the vocal cords and meals as the commonest triggers. Laryngeal cancer: targeted searching returned laryngeal squamous-cell-carcinoma biology and predictive-marker studies rather than laryngitis-primary risk cohorts, and any shared association is dominated by smoking and alcohol exposure that cannot be attributed to the laryngitis. Vocal-fold nodules and polyps: that window is authored by the chronic-laryngitis identity and rests on phonotrauma and occupational voice use rather than acute infection. Reopening condition: a laryngitis-primary cohort or series quantifying a distinct catalog secondary, or a governance decision separating this identity from the chronic form.
